forecasts.base_rate: Three reference classes, with the second now better instrumented than it was two days ago. Class A is capability-timing forecasts. The Goodheart Labs aggregate of Metaculus, Manifold and Kalshi inputs, fetched live 17 Aug 2026 and stamped 'as of August 16, 2026', gives a combined median AGI year of 2031 with an 80% interval of 2027-2042, which maps to roughly 30-35% of probability mass before 1 Jan 2030 under a lognormal-ish fit. Metaculus Q5121, 'first general AI system devised, tested and publicly announced', carried a January 2033 median with about 25% by 2029 from a pool above 1,800 forecasters at the last documented reading; that figure is mid-July and I could not fetch the live page, so it is carried forward unverified. Q3479 'weakly general AI' is much earlier at a June 2028 median, but its cognitive-only basket is a looser bar than this question's. Metaculus has scale and an audited near-term calibration record; Goodheart is an ensemble of five correlated series, not an independent sample. Class B is announcement-timing markets, which is the closest match to this question's actual resolution bar. Live Kalshi KXOAIAGI on 17 Aug prices OpenAI achieving AGI before 2030 at 44.8%, before 2028 at 19% and before 2027 at 9.8%, with under 900,000 dollars of cumulative volume on the near leg and essentially no trading over the last two sessions. That series is the right shape for this question - any credible lab, not just OpenAI - and it sits roughly twenty points above the OpenAI-only ladder on the comparable Jan 2028 leg, which is the strongest available evidence that the disjunctive bar carries real extra probability. Its illiquidity means I lift the anchor toward it only modestly. Polymarket's OpenAI-AGI-before-2027 sits near 11% (89% No), consistent with Kalshi. Manifold's 'AGI publicly demonstrated before 2030' near 50% dates to the 15 Jul 2026 snapshot and is not independently re-verified. Class C is the empirical announcement base rate: zero credible corporate AGI declarations in roughly 45 months since ChatGPT, with the near-misses (Huang's April 2026 'we've achieved AGI', Altman's 'basically built AGI') immediately contested and never institutionally adopted. Capability extrapolation, ARC-AGI-3 SOTA at a verified 30.2% and METR horizons doubling every 3-7 months, is consistent with 2027-2030 arrival, but the instruments saturate precisely where discrimination matters, and both Astra and Anthropic's Model 2 are now examples of frontier capability existing without a public declaration attached.

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change: Move: 16 to 15, CI from [9, 27] to [8, 26]. A 1pp reduction, second consecutive small step down. The 15-17 August window covers a Saturday, a Sunday and a Monday morning, so genuinely new consulting-sector reporting is close to nil: Consultancy.uk's news index as of 17 August still carries 14 August 2026 as its most recent dateline (client-experience piece, Clancy Consulting pre-pack notice, Ravical AI platform, Turner & Townsend five director hires), all of which were already priced into yesterday's 16. Two items surfaced in this run that were not logged before and both cut against the question. (1) The EU AI Act high-risk obligations became binding on 2 August 2026, covering Articles 9-17 for providers and Article 26 for deployers, with penalties up to EUR 15m or 3% of global turnover. Compliance requires AI system inventories, risk classification, technical documentation, conformity assessment, CE marking and EU database registration, and enterprise readiness is widely described as nascent. That is a mechanical increase in demand for exactly the regulatory, technical and economic advisory work this question asks about, arriving inside the forecast horizon and running in the opposite direction to the AI-displacement thesis. (2) Litigation filings surged in the first half of 2026 alongside a rise in AI-related claims and technology-company disputes, with 46% of corporate counsel reporting increased federal AI litigation exposure and 41% naming AI-enabled product launches as an emerging class action trigger. Antitrust, damages and platform-economics work is the core caseload of CRA, NERA, Cornerstone, Brattle and Compass Lexecon, so AI is currently generating more work for economic consultants than it is destroying. Confirming official data: the BLS Employment Situation for July 2026, released 7 August, shows total nonfarm payrolls -23,000, unemployment 4.1%, and professional and business services explicitly listed among industries showing 'little change over the month'; declines were concentrated in local government education (-50,000), retail trade (-19,000) and financial activities (-14,000), not professional services. No new firm disclosures in window; the only economic-consulting item remains the 12 August Cornerstone Research CEO succession, Bryan Ricchetti replacing Rahul Guha after a year-long planned transition, which is orderly and not distress. Net: nothing fired upward, one demand-positive regulatory deadline and one demand-positive litigation trend were added to the DOWN column, and the official employment series remains flat rather than contracting. A further 1pp step down is warranted; the CI floor eases to 8 because the down-side evidence is now stacking from independent channels (official output, official employment, buyer surveys, firm revenue, regulatory demand, litigation demand).
forecasts.base_rate: The reference class is professional-services sectors losing a third or more of revenue or employment within roughly six years, with the loss primarily attributed by multiple credible analyses to a single technology. The class is thin and the closest members fit badly. Travel agencies shed 40-50% of US employment, but over roughly fifteen years, and the automated function was transactional booking rather than judgement. Legal document review contracted sharply but was a discrete commoditised task inside a larger sector, not a sector. Typesetting, photo processing, stenography and directory assistance collapsed faster, but each was a craft occupation whose single output a machine reproduced exactly. In every clean member of the class, the automated thing was the whole product. Economic consultancy fails that test structurally: clients buy a bundle of quantitative analysis, testimony admissible before a court or regulator, relationship capital with counsel and agencies, political and legal cover, insurable accountability and a credential that survives cross-examination. AI compresses the analysis layer, plausibly a third to a half of delivered hours and less of the fee. The remaining layers should appreciate as machine-generated analysis proliferates, because signing your name to a number before a tribunal is a liability transfer no model performs. Three adjustments push up. AI attacks the pyramid economics that fund senior capacity, with Big Four UK graduate intake down 6-29%, McKinsey cutting toward 40,000 from 45,000-plus, Accenture exiting 11,000-plus under an $865m charge and BCG entry-level down 15%. Pricing is decoupling from hours, which can deflate sector revenue without any demand loss. And the May 2026 Anthropic ($1.5bn, Blackstone and Hellman & Friedman) and OpenAI ($4bn-plus, TPG, Advent, Bain Capital, Brookfield) services joint ventures are the first credibly capitalised AI-native entrants aimed at the consulting pool. Two adjustments push down harder than they did a week ago: AI is itself a demand generator, both through compliance (EU AI Act high-risk obligations binding from 2 August 2026) and through disputes (AI-related litigation filings surging in H1 2026), and the AI consulting segment is growing roughly 21-24% a year from about $10.9bn in 2025. Scope decides a lot: read narrowly as CRA, NERA, Cornerstone, Brattle, Compass Lexecon and Frontier, current evidence points the wrong way entirely. Outside view 5-12%, adjusted to 14-18% for the AI trajectory and entry-level compression, then discounted for the demanding 'primarily attributed to AI' bar and the two-credible-analyses requirement. Central 15%.

AI as litigation generator: filings surged in H1 2026 alongside AI-related claims, 46% of corporate counsel report increased federal AI litigation exposure and 41% cite AI-enabled product launches as an emerging class action trigger, feeding the antitrust, damages and platform-economics caseload that is the core of economic consulting

Official statistics show no contraction: BLS Employment Situation for July 2026 (released 7 Aug) lists professional and business services among industries with 'little change over the month' against total nonfarm -23,000, with losses concentrated in local government education, retail and financial activities; ONS Q2 2026 professional, scientific and technical output was +1.7%

Buyer intent moving toward, not away from, consultants: Source Global Research's 2026 survey shows AI-cautious buyers falling from 50% in 2025 to 23% in 2026 and deployed-or-eager rising from 15% to over 40%, with technology consulting still forecast above $400bn in 2026 and MCA/Oxford Economics at +5.7% for 2026 and +7.4% for 2027

That is a lower and softer bar than any market definition, for three reasons. First, labs have commercial and narrative incentives to claim the milestone and the term has no agreed operational meaning; Altman has already said publicly we are in the singularity and Hassabis has spoken of standing in the foothills of it. Second, a reference case exists: Jensen Huang said in March 2026 that AGI had been achieved and no one could agree what he meant; the claim failed only because Nvidia is a chip supplier rather than a lab and no researcher chorus followed. Combining a capability-based 72-79 percent with a declaration premium of roughly 8-12 points, then discounting for the credibility filter and for capex-bust or governance-freeze scenarios, gives a central in the mid-80s.

forecasts.base_rate: Outside view remains the anchor. The broad class is major-power amphibious assault or sustained naval blockade against defended territory since 1945: a handful of cases in eighty years, implying an annual hazard in the low single digits, which over the 3.4 years to 1 January 2030 gives roughly 3 to 8 percent before China-specific adjustment. The narrower and more informative class is Taiwan Strait coercion episodes since 1995: the 1995-96 missile crises, the August 2022 Pelosi encirclement, Joint Sword 2024A and 2024B, Strait Thunder 2025A and Justice Mission 2025. All involved declared closure areas, live fire or encirclement geometry; none converted into a sustained blockade or an assault on Taiwan proper. That is 0 for 7, each episode reversible, time-boxed to days and terminated on Beijing's own announcement. A second sub-class is now confirmed for a third year: PLA responses to Taiwan's annual Han Kuang exercise. In 2024, 2025 and now 2026 the PLA answered Han Kuang with rhetoric rather than a named counter-exercise, and Han Kuang 42 ran 5 to 14 August 2026 with only MND and Global Times commentary in reply. Joint Sword-2024B came in October, keyed to Lai's National Day speech, not to Han Kuang, so the October window rather than the August one is where the named-exercise hazard sits. The reference class is not static. The live hazard is shifting from invasion toward quarantine, a lower-threshold action framed as law enforcement, and the CCG standing patrol east of Taiwan under the Xiushan task force plus expansion of the Kinmen model, with 24 CCG entries into Kinmen restricted waters in 2026 to date, is the institutional scaffolding for it. But a CSIS- or RAND-style quarantine resolves this question YES only if it runs past 72 hours and two major agencies call it a blockade; a short, law-enforcement-branded interdiction probably would not. Capability trend is upward: Type 076 Sichuan delivery expected end-2026, the 2027 centenary readiness milestone inside the window. Prediction markets sit at or below this estimate: Polymarket prices invasion by end-2026 at 3.8 percent and any China-Taiwan military clash before 2027 at 7.1 percent, both with looser criteria and typical long-shot bias. Blending the classes and adding a premium for the 2028-29 convergence of capability, calendar and possible US distraction supports a central near 7 percent, right-skewed.

forecasts.base_rate: The governing reference class remains not 'blockbusters that reach $1.5B' but 'already-published box office milestones that are subsequently unpublished or restated below the threshold'. Theatrical cumulative grosses are monotonic in practice: refunds, comps and currency effects are absorbed inside reported figures rather than clawed back from prior totals. Across the modern tracked-release era there is no case of a major studio title's published worldwide cumulative being revised downward by anything approaching 26% after it cleared a round-number threshold. Routine revisions cluster in a 0.1%-2% band and arise from estimate-to-actual weekend corrections (rarely above 3% on a single frame, hence well under 1% of a $2.0B cumulative), currency retranslation of international grosses (which can move a territory by a few percent but seldom the global aggregate by more than 1%-2%, and is as likely up as down), and reclassification of re-releases or premium-format runs, which is material only for small titles. The largest genuinely contested restatements on record involve disputed territory reporting, most often China and India; even in the most-cited disputes the contested sums have been tens of millions on billion-dollar films, i.e. low single digits in percentage terms. Brand New Day's China total is $197.6M, about 9.8% of worldwide, so complete invalidation of the Chinese gross would still leave the film above $1.8B. The Rest of World residual is the single largest unitemised block at $374,968,249, 18.5% of worldwide, and voiding even that entirely leaves $1,646,863,751. A second class is source availability: both The Numbers and Box Office Mojo have operated continuously for over two decades, and because the question resolves on either, both would have to fail simultaneously within a four-and-a-half-month window. Box Office Mojo's current site-wide 2026 staleness is a live demonstration that single-source failure happens, and equally a demonstration of why the either/or resolution clause matters. Combining a sub-1-in-10,000 hazard of a 26%-plus downward restatement with a dual-source failure hazard of similar order leaves residual failure probability well below 0.1%.

The prior treated the retreat from 5 percent as evidence that trigger 5 had not fired; that retreat has now reversed. The level still sits well short of the 5.5 percent revise-down threshold, but the direction of travel matters for a question whose upside case leans on Healey routing roughly GBP 9bn a year of extra investment borrowing through the fiscal-rule asset offset. Treasury officials are already reported as warning that investors may read Burnham's approach as lacking a genuine binding constraint. Higher term premia raise the price of exactly the public capital deepening that the bull case requires.

NEGATIVE TWO. The Hormuz deadlock hardened rather than resolved. Brent stood at $88.31 on 17 August 2026, down 0.24 percent on the day but up more than 5 percent across the week, as Iran and Oman failed to reach agreement on reopening the strait and Washington escalated. Bessent has said the US will impose unprecedented economic measures while maintaining the naval blockade of Iranian ports, with further announcements expected this week. Brent below $100 means trigger 6 still has not fired on price, but a week of rising prices on a failed deal shifts weight toward EY's closed-strait scenario, in which UK GDP grows 0.5 percent in 2026 and contracts 0.2 percent in 2027.

NEGATIVE THREE, structural and the most relevant to the 2030s. UK output per hour rose 0.9 percent q/q in Q1 2026 but only 0.4 percent year on year, after a 0.4 percent annual fall in the prior period. A 0.4 percent y/y trend run rate is less than half the OBR's 1.0 percent underlying assumption. Corroborating this, Bank staff estimates in the April 2026 Monetary Policy Report put potential supply growth at around 0.3-0.4 percent per quarter, and Bailey's 14 July 2026 Mansion House speech described post-crisis potential supply growth as having halved to around 1.25 percent a year from above 2.5 percent pre-2008. Both official supply-side anchors now sit below the 1.5 percent bar rather than straddling it. The ONS productivity flash estimate is due 18 August 2026, one day outside this window.

POSITIVE ONE. The Resolution Foundation's 13 August release confirmed the UK was the fastest-growing G7 economy in the first half of 2026, with combined growth of 1.0 percent across Q1 and Q2, and GDP per capita up 0.4 percent in Q2. That is real cyclical outperformance. But the same release put GDP per capita 6.6 percent below its pre-pandemic trend, which is a reminder of how large the level shortfall is and how little of it is being recovered. Net, this is a wash rather than an upgrade.

TRIGGER CHECK. (1) UP if the 28 October OBR forecast leaves trend productivity at 1.0 percent or higher, or IMF/OECD lift potential above 1.5 percent: DID NOT FIRE. The OBR forecast commissioned for 28 October 2026 remains pending; the IMF Article IV concluded 16 July still holds potential at 1.4 percent. Reporting continues to point to downgrades across every forecast year to 2030 on trend productivity revisions. (2) UP if AI productivity contributions broaden beyond AI-producing sectors, or ONS adoption depth exceeds 1.6 tools per adopter: DID NOT FIRE. No new ONS or BoE industry evidence in the window. The large headline numbers in circulation, Microsoft-commissioned GBP 550bn by 2035, PwC's 10 percent higher GDP by 2030, the AI Opportunities Action Plan's GBP 400bn by 2030, are all commissioned scenario work, not measured outturns, and none is new. (3) UP if business investment posts a second consecutive quarter of 1.5 percent or better, or BCC capex intentions recover above 25 percent, or the 10-year gilt falls below 4 percent: DID NOT FIRE. Q3 business investment is not published until late 2026; BCC intentions remain at 17 percent from fieldwork of 11 May to 8 June; the gilt went the wrong way to 5.04 percent. (4) DOWN if Q3 2026 GDP comes in at 0.1 percent q/q or lower: NOT YET TESTABLE, the July monthly print lands 11 September. (5) DOWN if the 10-year gilt exceeds 5.5 percent or the Budget delivers capital-led consolidation: DID NOT FIRE but MOVED ADVERSELY, 5.04 percent on 14 August is a fresh high, and Budget reporting still points to business-rates rebalancing toward smaller firms rather than capital cuts. (6) DOWN if Hormuz stays disrupted into 2027 with Brent sustained above $100, or labour demand keeps deteriorating: PARTIALLY FIRED, unchanged from the prior. Hormuz remains closed with talks stalled and Brent up 5 percent on the week, but at $88.31 it is far below $100.

NET REASONING. The arithmetic is unchanged and remains the whole question. Roughly 1.0 percent trend productivity, and arguably nearer 0.4 percent on the latest y/y outturn, plus roughly 0.3-0.5 percent labour supply growth as natural change turns negative from 2026 and net migration settles near the ONS 230,000 long-run assumption, gives potential in the 1.3-1.5 percent range with the central point just under the bar. A decade arithmetic mean is then dragged asymmetrically by recession years. What moved in this window was not the central arithmetic but the tail: a fresh gilt high raises the cost of the investment-led upside path, a failed Hormuz negotiation raises the odds of a 2027 contraction feeding into an early-2030s starting base, and the productivity y/y print at 0.4 percent sits below rather than at the OBR anchor. One point down is the right size for two days of thin, directionally consistent news on a fourteen-year structural question. The CI shifts down by one point and keeps its 27-point width, since nothing in the window resolved any structural uncertainty. The 18 August productivity flash and the 20 August Blue Book 2026 GDP impacts article are the next scheduled tests.
forecasts.base_rate: The naive outside view flatters the question. UK decade averages for annual real GDP growth were about 2.2 percent in the 1990s, 1.8 percent in the 2000s and 2.0 percent in the 2010s, with the 2020s running near 1.0 percent to date, so three of the last four decades cleared 1.5 percent and the unadjusted base rate is roughly 60-75 percent. That reference class is contaminated. Pre-2008 decades rested on labour productivity growth near 2 percent a year plus rapid labour force expansion from rising female participation and later EU accession migration; neither driver is available for the 2030s. The 2010s figure is itself misleading, resting on a deep post-crisis output gap that mechanically flattered measured growth through recovery rather than trend. Bailey's 14 July 2026 Mansion House speech makes the break explicit: potential supply growth averaged above 2.5 percent a year from 1990 to the financial crisis and halved to around 1.25 percent in the decade after it. The forward decomposition is the better anchor. Potential growth equals trend productivity plus trend labour input. The OBR cut underlying medium-term productivity growth to 1.0 percent a year from 1.3 percent in November 2025 and retained 1.0 percent in the March 2026 EFO, with further downgrades to growth in every year to 2030 now trailed for 28 October. The IMF 2026 Article IV, concluded 16 July 2026, assessed UK potential growth at 1.4 percent. Bank staff estimates in the April 2026 Monetary Policy Report put potential supply growth around 0.3-0.4 percent per quarter. Realised productivity is running below all of these: output per hour was up just 0.4 percent y/y in Q1 2026 after a 0.4 percent annual fall in the prior period. On labour supply, ONS 2024-based projections have natural change negative from 2026 onward, net migration falling to 138,000 in 2026 before stabilising at a long-run 230,000 from 2028, and the UK population growing 2.3 million between 2025 and 2039 with migration accounting for essentially all of it. That implies working-age population growth of roughly 0.3-0.5 percent a year across the 2030s, lower if inactivity keeps drifting up from 9.11 million. Adding roughly 1.0 percent productivity to roughly 0.3-0.5 percent labour supply gives potential near 1.3-1.5 percent, with the central estimate marginally below the threshold. Shocks are asymmetric against the question: a decade arithmetic mean is dragged down far more by one recession year than lifted by one boom year, and the 2030s carry non-trivial odds of at least one recession, energy shock, climate disruption or fiscal event. Medium-term official growth projections for OECD economies have also systematically overshot outturns since 2008.
